questions.prompt: Which of the following statements are true? Here $\mathbb Q$ is the additive group of rational numbers.

options.A: $\mathbb Q$ has countably many subgroups.
options.B: $\mathbb Q$ has uncountably many subsets.
options.C: Every finitely generated subgroup of $\mathbb Q$ is cyclic.
options.D: $\mathbb Q$ is isomorphic to $\mathbb Q\times\mathbb Q$ as groups.

hints: Compare subsets of primes with subgroups generated by reciprocals of those primes.
Put finitely many rational generators over a common denominator. To compare the groups, examine the quotient by twice the cyclic subgroup generated by one nonzero element, or rational rank.
questions.solution: B is true by Cantor’s theorem: the power set of a countably infinite set has cardinality $2^{\aleph_0}$. For every set $S$ of primes let $H_S=\mathbb Z[1/p:p\in S]$, regarded additively. The rational number $1/p$ belongs to $H_S$ exactly when $p\in S$, so distinct prime sets give distinct subgroups. Thus there are uncountably many subgroups, and A is false. If the generators are $a_1/d,\ldots,a_k/d$, their generated subgroup is $(\gcd(a_1,\ldots,a_k)/d)\mathbb Z$, proving C. Any homomorphism between rational vector spaces considered as additive groups is $\mathbb Q$-linear: division by each nonzero integer is unique. Therefore an isomorphism in D would be a vector-space isomorphism between dimensions one and two, which is impossible.
questions.theory: An additive subgroup need not be finitely generated even when its ambient group is countable. Countability of elements says nothing comparable about the number of subsets or subgroups: the power set of a countably infinite set is uncountable. Localization at a selected set of primes gives a useful family of rational subgroups with recoverable prime denominators. A finitely generated rational subgroup is cyclic because a common denominator reduces the problem to subgroups of $\mathbb Z$, all of which are generated by one integer; Bézout’s identity identifies that integer as a greatest common divisor. The group $\mathbb Q$ is uniquely divisible: for every nonzero integer $n$, multiplication by $n$ is bijective. This makes its additive-group homomorphisms automatically rational-linear. Rational dimension, rather than mere cardinality, consequently distinguishes $\mathbb Q$ from $\mathbb Q^2$.

similar_questions.prompt: Find the additive subgroup generated by $2/9$ and $5/12$.
similar_questions.solution: A common denominator is $36$, giving generators $8/36$ and $15/36$. Since $\gcd(8,15)=1$, Bézout’s identity gives $\langle2/9,5/12\rangle=(1/36)\mathbb Z$.

similar_questions.prompt: Are the additive groups $\mathbb Q^2$ and $\mathbb Q^3$ isomorphic?
similar_questions.solution: Every additive homomorphism commutes with multiplication by integers and unique division by integers, hence with rational scalars. An additive isomorphism would therefore preserve rational dimension. Since the dimensions are $2$ and $3$, no such isomorphism exists.

questions.prompt: Let $SL_2(\mathbb Z)=\{\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}\in M_2(\mathbb Z):ad-bc=1\}$. For any prime $p$, let $\Gamma(p)=\{\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}\in SL_2(\mathbb Z):a\equiv d\equiv1\pmod p,\ c\equiv b\equiv0\pmod p\}$. Which statements are true?

options.A: $\Gamma(p)$ is a subgroup of $SL_2(\mathbb Z)$.
options.B: $\Gamma(p)$ is not a normal subgroup of $SL_2(\mathbb Z)$.
options.C: $\Gamma(p)$ has at least two elements.

hints: View entrywise reduction modulo $p$ as a group homomorphism.
Identify its kernel, and compare the identity with $\begin{pmatrix}1&p\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$.
questions.solution: The map $\rho:SL_2(\mathbb Z)\to SL_2(\mathbb F_p)$ reducing entries modulo $p$ respects matrix multiplication and determinants. Its kernel is exactly $\Gamma(p)$. A kernel is a normal subgroup, so A is true and B false. The identity and $\begin{pmatrix}1&p\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$ are distinct members, proving C. In fact all $\begin{pmatrix}1&kp\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$ for $k\in\mathbb Z$ belong to it. Every integer matrix is an element of the countable set $\mathbb Z^4$, so every subset, including $\Gamma(p)$, is at most countable. D is false.
questions.theory: For groups $G,H$, a homomorphism $\phi:G\to H$ preserves products and has a kernel $\ker\phi=\{g:\phi(g)=e_H\}$. The kernel is always a normal subgroup because $\phi(ghg^{-1})=e_H$ whenever $\phi(h)=e_H$. Reduction of matrix entries modulo an integer is compatible with addition and multiplication, and therefore with matrix multiplication and determinant. The principal congruence subgroup consists precisely of matrices reducing to the identity. Surjectivity of the reduction map is not needed to prove that its kernel is normal. Explicit unipotent matrices establish nontriviality and infinitude without a counting formula. Finally, a finite Cartesian product of countable sets is countable, so integer matrix groups and their subgroups cannot be uncountable. Distinguish countability of a group from the possible uncountability of its collection of subgroups.

similar_questions.prompt: Show that $\{A\in GL_2(\mathbb Z):A\equiv I\pmod3\}$ is normal in $GL_2(\mathbb Z)$.
similar_questions.solution: Reduction gives a homomorphism $GL_2(\mathbb Z)\to GL_2(\mathbb F_3)$ because integer invertible matrices have determinant $\pm1$, still nonzero modulo $3$. The stated set is its kernel, so it is normal.

similar_questions.prompt: Give infinitely many elements of $\Gamma(5)$.
similar_questions.solution: For every integer $k$, $A_k=\begin{pmatrix}1&5k\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$ has determinant one and reduces to the identity modulo five. Different integers give different upper-right entries, so the set is infinite; it is countable as a subset of $\mathbb Z^4$.

questions.prompt: Let $G$ be a finite group. Which statements are true?

options.A: If $g\in G$ has order $m$ and $n\ge1$ divides $m$, then $G$ has a subgroup of order $n$.
options.B: If for any two subgroups $A,B$ of $G$, either $A\subset B$ or $B\subset A$, then $G$ is cyclic.
options.C: If $G$ is cyclic, then for any subgroups $A,B$ of $G$, either $A\subset B$ or $B\subset A$.
options.D: If for every positive integer $m$ dividing $|G|$, $G$ has a subgroup of order $m$, then $G$ is abelian.

hints: Use subgroups of the cyclic group generated by $g$ for A. Test C on a cyclic group of composite order with two distinct prime factors.
For B choose a cyclic subgroup of maximal order and compare it with every $\langle x\rangle$. For D test $S_3$.
questions.solution: For A the subgroup $\langle g^{m/n}\rangle$ has order $n$, so A holds. For B choose $h$ with maximal element order. The hypothesis compares $\langle h\rangle$ with $\langle x\rangle$ for every $x\in G$. If $\langle h\rangle\subseteq\langle x\rangle$, maximality of its order forces equality; otherwise $\langle x\rangle\subseteq\langle h\rangle$. Thus every element belongs to $\langle h\rangle$, and $G$ is cyclic. C fails for $C_6$, whose order-two and order-three subgroups are incomparable. D fails for the nonabelian group $S_3$: it has subgroups of orders $1,2,3,6$, every divisor of its order.
questions.theory: In a cyclic group of order $m$, the element $g^k$ has order $m/\gcd(m,k)$, and there is exactly one subgroup of each order dividing $m$. Uniqueness at a given order does not mean all subgroups form a chain: inclusion corresponds to divisibility of their orders. For example, orders two and three are incomparable. A finite group whose subgroup lattice is totally ordered must be cyclic, because a cyclic subgroup maximal by order contains every cyclic subgroup and hence every element. Finiteness is essential to this maximal-order argument. Lagrange’s theorem gives the necessary divisibility of subgroup orders, but existence of subgroups for all divisors is a weaker property than commutativity. Small permutation groups are useful counterexamples: $S_3$ has all possible divisor orders while two transpositions fail to commute.

similar_questions.prompt: List the subgroup orders of $C_{12}$ and determine whether its subgroups form a chain.
similar_questions.solution: The orders are $1,2,3,4,6,12$, with exactly one subgroup for each. The order-three subgroup is not contained in the order-four subgroup, nor conversely, so the lattice is not a chain.

similar_questions.prompt: If a finite group has exactly two subgroups, prove it is cyclic of prime order.
similar_questions.solution: The subgroups must be $\{e\}$ and $G$. Any nonidentity $g$ generates a nontrivial subgroup, hence generates $G$. If its order were composite, the cyclic group would have a proper nontrivial subgroup corresponding to a proper divisor. Thus its order is prime.

It is maximal exactly when the quotient is a field. Preimages of prime ideals under ring homomorphisms are prime, while surjectivity here additionally guarantees a nonzero preimage ideal from the nonzero ideal $Q$. The first isomorphism theorem identifies $R/f^{-1}(Q)$ with $S/Q$ for a surjective map. In a principal ideal domain, nonzero prime ideals are maximal, but the zero prime need not be. A finite integral domain is a field because multiplication by a nonzero element is injective and therefore surjective. Polynomial identities pass to quotients; cancellation in a domain can turn such an identity into an explicit inverse formula.

similar_questions.prompt: If a commutative ring satisfies $x^3=x$ for every $x$, show that all its prime ideals are maximal.
similar_questions.solution: For a prime ideal $P$, the quotient is a domain satisfying the same identity. For any nonzero $a$, $a(a^2-1)=0$ forces $a^2=1$, so $a^{-1}=a$. Thus the quotient is a field, and $P$ is maximal.

similar_questions.prompt: For reduction $f:\mathbb Z\to\mathbb Z/12\mathbb Z$, find the preimage of the prime ideal generated by the class of $2$.
similar_questions.solution: The ideal consists of even residue classes. Its preimage is $2\mathbb Z$. The quotient $\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z$ is a field, so this preimage is both prime and maximal. The corresponding quotient of $\mathbb Z/12\mathbb Z$ is also $\mathbb F_2$.

questions.prompt: Consider $f(x)=x^2+3x-1$. Which statements are true?

options.A: $f$ is irreducible over $\mathbb Z[\sqrt{13}]$.
options.B: $f$ is irreducible over $\mathbb Q$.
options.C: $f$ is reducible over $\mathbb Q[\sqrt{13}]$.
options.D: $\mathbb Z[\sqrt{13}]$ is a unique factorization domain.

hints: Compute the two roots and check which coefficient rings contain them.
A monic quadratic can factor into positive-degree polynomials over this domain only if it has a root in the domain. To test UFD, consider integral closure.
questions.solution: The discriminant is $13$, so the roots are $(-3\pm\sqrt{13})/2$. They are not rational, proving B, but lie in the field $\mathbb Q[\sqrt{13}]$, proving C. Neither root lies in $\mathbb Z[\sqrt{13}]$, since its coefficients in the rational basis $1,\sqrt{13}$ are nonintegers. A factorization of the monic quadratic in this ring into linear factors has unit leading coefficients; rescaling by those units gives monic linear factors and hence a root in the ring. A constant nonunit cannot divide a monic polynomial. Thus A holds. D is false: $\alpha=(1+\sqrt{13})/2$ lies in the fraction field and satisfies the monic equation $\alpha^2-\alpha-3=0$, yet is absent from $\mathbb Z[\sqrt{13}]$. This ring is not integrally closed, whereas every UFD is integrally closed.
questions.theory: Irreducibility depends on the coefficient ring. Over a field, a quadratic is reducible exactly when it has a root in that field, and the discriminant detects rational roots. Over an integral domain the same root test applies to monic quadratics: factors of positive degree must be linear, and their leading coefficients multiply to one, so they are units and can be normalized. Monicity also rules out a constant nonunit factor. An element of the fraction field is integral over a ring if it satisfies a monic polynomial with coefficients in the ring. A domain is integrally closed when all such elements already belong to it. Every unique factorization domain is integrally closed. For squarefree $d\equiv1\pmod4$, the element $(1+\sqrt d)/2$ is integral over $\mathbb Z[\sqrt d]$ but generally absent, providing a quick obstruction to unique factorization.

similar_questions.prompt: Is $x^2-x-1$ irreducible over $\mathbb Z[\sqrt5]$ and over $\mathbb Q(\sqrt5)$?
similar_questions.solution: Its roots are $(1\pm\sqrt5)/2$. Neither belongs to $\mathbb Z[\sqrt5]$, so monicity makes the polynomial irreducible there. Both belong to $\mathbb Q(\sqrt5)$, where the polynomial factors into the two corresponding linear factors.

similar_questions.prompt: Prove that $\mathbb Z[\sqrt{17}]$ is not a UFD.
similar_questions.solution: The fraction-field element $\beta=(1+\sqrt{17})/2$ satisfies $\beta^2-\beta-4=0$ and is therefore integral. It is not in $\mathbb Z[\sqrt{17}]$ because both basis coefficients are halves. The ring is not integrally closed, so cannot be a UFD.

questions.prompt: Let $p$ be an odd prime with $p\equiv2\pmod3$, and let $\mathbb F_p$ be the field with $p$ elements. Define $E=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb F_p\times\mathbb F_p:y^2=x^3+1\}$. Which statements are true?

options.A: $E$ has at least two elements.
options.B: $E$ has at most $2p$ elements.
options.C: $E$ can have $p^2$ elements.

hints: For a fixed $x$ there are at most two square roots of $x^3+1$.
Use $\gcd(3,p-1)=1$ to show that cubing permutes $\mathbb F_p$. Count by fixing $y$.
questions.solution: The multiplicative group $\mathbb F_p^\times$ has order $p-1$, relatively prime to $3$. Hence $x\mapsto x^3$ is bijective on $\mathbb F_p^\times$, and also on all of $\mathbb F_p$ after including zero. For each of the $p$ choices of $y$, the equation $x^3=y^2-1$ has exactly one solution. Consequently $|E|=p$. Since an odd prime congruent to two modulo three is at least five, A and B hold, while C and D are false. Independently, $(0,1)$ and $(0,-1)$ establish A directly, and the degree-two equation in $y$ gives the upper bound in B.
questions.theory: The nonzero elements of a finite field form a cyclic multiplicative group. On a finite cyclic group of order $m$, the power map $u\mapsto u^k$ is bijective exactly when $\gcd(k,m)=1$; Bézout’s identity gives an inverse power. The map extends to a permutation of the whole field by sending zero to zero. Counting solutions of an equation in two variables is often easiest by fixing the variable for which the other equation has a unique solution. Here the congruence condition on $p$ makes cubing bijective, so the count is exactly $p$, not merely bounded by $2p$. A polynomial of degree two over a field has at most two roots, including the possibility of one repeated root or no roots. This root bound proves an upper bound but should not be mistaken for equality.

similar_questions.prompt: Count $(x,y)\in\mathbb F_{11}^2$ satisfying $y^2=x^3+4$.
similar_questions.solution: Since $\gcd(3,10)=1$, cubing is a bijection of $\mathbb F_{11}$. Every $y$ determines exactly one $x$ from $x^3=y^2-4$. There are eleven values of $y$, hence eleven solutions.

similar_questions.prompt: Count $(x,y)\in\mathbb F_7^2$ satisfying $y^2=x^5+2$.
similar_questions.solution: The fifth-power map is bijective because $\gcd(5,6)=1$. For each of the seven $y$ values, $x^5=y^2-2$ has one solution. Thus there are exactly seven pairs. No assumption that squaring is bijective is needed.

questions.prompt: Consider $A=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2:(x-1)(x-2)(y-3)(y+4)=0\}$. Which statements are true?

options.A: $A$ is connected.
options.B: $A$ is compact.
options.C: $A$ is closed.

hints: The zero set is a union of four entire lines.
Use their intersections for connectedness and the continuous polynomial for closedness. Test boundedness and a point away from all four lines.
questions.solution: The set is the union of the vertical lines $x=1,x=2$ and horizontal lines $y=3,y=-4$. Each line is path connected and the horizontal lines meet both vertical lines. Any two points can therefore be joined by a polygonal path along these lines, proving A. The polynomial defining $A$ is continuous, and $A$ is its inverse image of the closed set $\{0\}$, so C holds. The set contains entire lines and is unbounded; Heine–Borel makes B false. It is proper and closed, hence cannot be dense in $\mathbb R^2$; for example, a sufficiently small ball about $(0,0)$ avoids all four lines. D is false.
questions.theory: A product of real factors vanishes if and only if at least one factor vanishes, so factored polynomial zero sets can often be understood as unions of simpler geometric sets. A continuous function has closed zero set because the singleton $\{0\}$ is closed. Connected sets with a common point have a connected union, and a chain of intersections can similarly establish connectedness of a finite union. In this example one can prove the stronger property of path connectedness by constructing line-segment paths. In Euclidean space, compactness is equivalent to being closed and bounded, so closedness alone is insufficient. Density means the closure is the whole ambient space. A closed proper subset is therefore never dense. These properties concern the ambient topology and should be checked independently rather than inferred from a sketch alone.

similar_questions.prompt: Determine whether the union of the two coordinate axes in $\mathbb R^2$ is connected, closed, compact, and dense.
similar_questions.solution: It is the zero set of $xy$, so closed. Both axes are path connected and meet at the origin, so their union is path connected. It is unbounded, hence not compact, and proper closed, hence not dense.

similar_questions.prompt: Determine connectedness and closedness of $B=\{(x,y):(x-1)(x+1)=0\}$.
similar_questions.solution: This is the union of the disjoint vertical lines $x=1$ and $x=-1$. It is a polynomial zero set and therefore closed. The intersections of $B$ with the open half-planes $x>0$ and $x<0$ are nonempty disjoint relatively open sets covering $B$, so it is disconnected.

questions.prompt: Let $X$ be nonempty and let $\tau_1,\tau_2$ be topologies on $X$ such that $\tau_2\subset\tau_1$. Which statements imply $\tau_1=\tau_2$?

options.A: $(X,\tau_1)$ is compact and $\tau_1$ is $T_2$ (Hausdorff).
options.B: $(X,\tau_1)$ is compact and $\tau_2$ is $T_2$ (Hausdorff).
options.C: The connected components of $(X,\tau_1)$ and $(X,\tau_2)$ are the same.
options.D: For every $A\subseteq X$, its closure in $(X,\tau_2)$ is contained in its closure in $(X,\tau_1)$.

hints: The identity from the finer topology to the coarser topology is continuous.
A continuous bijection from compact to Hausdorff is a homeomorphism. Also compare closures under inclusion of topologies.
questions.solution: For B, the identity $\operatorname{id}:(X,\tau_1)\to(X,\tau_2)$ is a continuous bijection from compact to Hausdorff, hence a homeomorphism; the topologies coincide. Always $\overline A^{\tau_1}\subseteq\overline A^{\tau_2}$ because $\tau_1$ is finer. D supplies the reverse containment for every subset, so the closure operators, closed sets, and topologies coincide. A fails on a two-point set with $\tau_1$ discrete and $\tau_2$ indiscrete: the finer topology is compact Hausdorff but the topologies differ. C fails on $X=\mathbb R$, taking $\tau_1$ usual and $\tau_2$ indiscrete. Both spaces are connected, so both have the single component $X$, but the topologies differ.
questions.theory: Inclusion $\tau_2\subseteq\tau_1$ means $\tau_1$ is finer and the identity map from the finer space to the coarser one is continuous. The compact-to-Hausdorff theorem says a continuous bijection from a compact space to a Hausdorff space is a homeomorphism: images of closed sets are compact and hence closed in the Hausdorff target. The target, rather than only the source, must be Hausdorff for this argument. A finer topology makes closures smaller, because more closed sets are available in the defining intersection. A closure operator determines the closed sets through the condition $\overline A=A$, and hence determines the topology. Connected components record maximal connected subsets and are much coarser information than the full family of open sets; equal component decompositions need not imply equal topologies.

similar_questions.prompt: If a compact topology $\tau$ on $X$ is finer than a Hausdorff topology $\sigma$, prove equality.
similar_questions.solution: The identity $(X,\tau)\to(X,\sigma)$ is continuous and bijective. Every $\tau$-closed set is compact, so its image is $\sigma$-closed. The inverse is continuous, making the identity a homeomorphism and giving $\tau=\sigma$.

similar_questions.prompt: Give two distinct topologies on one set having equal closure operators.
similar_questions.solution: This is impossible. In each topology the closed subsets are exactly the fixed points of the closure operator. Equal operators imply the same closed sets; taking complements then gives the same open sets and hence equal topologies.

questions.prompt: The two-point boundary value problem $y^{\prime\prime}(x)+\lambda y(x)=0$ for $x\in(0,\pi)$, $y(0)=y(\pi)=0$, has the trivial solution $y=0$. It also has a nontrivial solution for

options.A: No values of $\lambda\in\mathbb R$.
options.B: $\lambda=1$.
options.C: $\lambda=n^2$ for all $n\in\mathbb N$, $n>1$.

hints: Separate the cases $\lambda>0$, $\lambda=0$, and $\lambda<0$.
For positive $\lambda$, the first boundary condition leaves a sine; the second requires $\sin(\pi\sqrt\lambda)=0$.
questions.solution: If $\lambda=\mu^2>0$, the general solution is $a\cos(\mu x)+b\sin(\mu x)$. The condition at zero gives $a=0$, and a nonzero solution exists exactly when $\sin(\mu\pi)=0$, that is, $\mu=n\ge1$. Thus $\lambda=n^2$, with solutions $b\sin(nx)$, proving B and C. When $\lambda=0$, $y=a+bx$ and the two boundary conditions force $a=b=0$. When $\lambda=-\mu^2<0$, the first condition gives $y=b\sinh(\mu x)$ and the second forces $b=0$. Therefore A and D are false.
questions.theory: A homogeneous boundary value problem always has the zero solution; the spectral question is which parameter values permit a nonzero one. For the Dirichlet problem $-y^{\prime\prime}=\lambda y$ on an interval of length $L$, the eigenvalues are $(n\pi/L)^2$ for positive integers $n$, and eigenfunctions are sine functions. These conclusions require both endpoint conditions and regular solutions on the closed interval. A quick sign check comes from integration by parts: $\int|y^{\prime}|^2=\lambda\int|y|^2$, since the boundary term vanishes. Any nonzero Dirichlet solution therefore has $\lambda>0$. The zero parameter must be checked separately because the trigonometric formula degenerates there. Although the zero function satisfies every parameter, it is not an eigenfunction and cannot establish an eigenvalue.

similar_questions.prompt: Find the eigenvalues of $y^{\prime\prime}+\lambda y=0$, $y(0)=y(2)=0$.
similar_questions.solution: For positive $\lambda$, $y=b\sin(\sqrt\lambda x)$. A nonzero $b$ requires $2\sqrt\lambda=n\pi$, so the eigenvalues are $n^2\pi^2/4$, $n\ge1$. The zero and negative cases give only the zero solution.

similar_questions.prompt: For $y^{\prime\prime}+\lambda y=0$, $y(0)=0$, $y^{\prime}(\pi)=0$, find positive eigenvalues.
similar_questions.solution: The first condition gives $y=b\sin(\sqrt\lambda x)$. Then $y^{\prime}(\pi)=b\sqrt\lambda\cos(\pi\sqrt\lambda)=0$. Nonzero solutions require $\sqrt\lambda=n+1/2$, $n=0,1,\ldots$, so $\lambda=(n+1/2)^2$.

questions.prompt: Let $A$ be an $n\times n$ matrix with distinct eigenvalues $(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_n)$ and corresponding linearly independent eigenvectors $\{\mathbf v_1,\ldots,\mathbf v_n\}$. Consider the nonhomogeneous differential equation $\mathbf x^{\prime}(t)=A\mathbf x(t)+e^{\lambda_1t}\mathbf v_1$.

options.A: Does not have a solution of the form $e^{\lambda_1t}\mathbf a$ for any vector $\mathbf a\in\mathbb R^n$.
options.B: Has a solution of the form $e^{\lambda_1t}\mathbf a$ for some vector $\mathbf a\in\mathbb R^n$.
options.C: Has a solution of the form $e^{\lambda_1t}\mathbf a+te^{\lambda_1t}\mathbf b$ for some vectors $\mathbf a,\mathbf b\in\mathbb R^n$.
options.D: Does not have a solution of the form $e^{\lambda_1t}\mathbf a+te^{\lambda_1t}\mathbf b$ for any vectors $\mathbf a,\mathbf b\in\mathbb R^n$.

hints: Express a proposed constant vector in the eigenvector basis.
The operator $\lambda_1 I-A$ kills $\mathbf v_1$ and has range spanned by the other eigenvectors. Try $te^{\lambda_1t}\mathbf v_1$.
questions.solution: For $\mathbf x=e^{\lambda_1t}\mathbf a$, substitution requires $(\lambda_1I-A)\mathbf a=\mathbf v_1$. Expand $\mathbf a=\sum_jc_j\mathbf v_j$; the left side is $\sum_{j>1}(\lambda_1-\lambda_j)c_j\mathbf v_j$ and has no $\mathbf v_1$ component. This is impossible, proving A and refuting B. Direct differentiation of $\mathbf x=te^{\lambda_1t}\mathbf v_1$ gives $\mathbf x^{\prime}=e^{\lambda_1t}\mathbf v_1+\lambda_1te^{\lambda_1t}\mathbf v_1=A\mathbf x+e^{\lambda_1t}\mathbf v_1$. Thus C holds with $\mathbf a=0$, $\mathbf b=\mathbf v_1$, while D is false. As usual in the displayed real-vector formulation, the matrix and eigenpair used in the equation are understood in the real setting.
questions.theory: For a constant-coefficient linear system, eigenvectors belonging to distinct eigenvalues are linearly independent; a full eigenvector basis diagonalizes the system. A forcing exponential whose exponent is not an eigenvalue admits a particular solution with the same exponential and a constant vector obtained by solving a linear algebra equation. When the forcing is along an eigenvector with the same eigenvalue, resonance prevents that simple ansatz. Multiplication by $t$ supplies the missing derivative term, just as for scalar linear equations. The range obstruction is especially transparent in a diagonal eigenvector basis. Distinct eigenvalues matter: with a Jordan block, an eigenvector may lie in the range of the shifted operator, changing the constant-vector ansatz. Particular solutions can always be supplemented by arbitrary homogeneous solutions; existence of one particular form does not assert uniqueness.

similar_questions.prompt: Solve $x^{\prime}=3x+e^{3t}$.

similar_questions.prompt: Find a particular solution of $\mathbf x^{\prime}=\operatorname{diag}(2,5)\mathbf x+e^{2t}(1,0)^T$.

questions.solution: At $t=0$, the two vectors are $(1,1,0)^T$ and $(0,1,1)^T$. If $a\mathbf y_1+b\mathbf y_2=0$, its first coordinate at zero gives $a=0$ and its third gives $b=0$. questions.theory: The solutions of a homogeneous linear system form a vector space because differentiation and multiplication by the coefficient matrix are linear. For a continuous $n\times n$ coefficient matrix on an interval, the initial-value theorem gives a unique solution for every initial vector at a fixed time. Evaluation at that time is consequently a linear isomorphism from the solution space to the underlying $n$-dimensional vector space. Linear independence of solution functions can therefore be checked at one common time using their initial vectors. A fundamental set contains exactly $n$ independent solutions, and arranging them as columns gives a fundamental matrix. Individual solutions may have distinct exponential factors, but independence is a property of the full vector functions. Two independent vectors in a three-dimensional solution space are extendible to a basis but do not themselves form one.

questions.solution: With the convention $Au_{xx}+2Bu_{xy}+Cu_{yy}$, the discriminant is $\Delta=B^2-AC$. In (i), $A=B=1$, $C=1-\operatorname{sgn}(y)$, so $\Delta=\operatorname{sgn}(y)$. It is hyperbolic for $y>0$ and elliptic for $y<0$; B holds and A fails. In (ii), $A=y$, $B=0$, $C=x$, hence $\Delta=-xy$. The product $xy$ is positive in I and III and negative in II and IV, proving C and refuting D. On a nonzero point of a coordinate axis (ii) is parabolic; at the origin its entire principal part vanishes.
questions.theory: A second-order linear equation in two variables is classified locally by the quadratic form of its highest derivatives. Writing the mixed coefficient as $2B$ is crucial: if one instead writes $Bu_{xy}$, the discriminant becomes $B^2-4AC$. The sign convention is hyperbolic for a positive discriminant, elliptic for a negative one, and parabolic for zero when the principal form is not identically zero. Multiplying the equation by a nonzero scalar does not alter its type because the discriminant is multiplied by the square of that scalar. Variable coefficients allow the type to change across curves, as in mixed-type equations. At a point where all highest-order coefficients vanish, the usual three-way classification is degenerate. Lower-order terms do not determine the elliptic, hyperbolic, or parabolic type.

questions.prompt: Consider the Cauchy problem $u_{xy}=0$ for $|x|<1$, $0<y<1$, with $u(x,x^2)=0$ and $u_y(x,x^2)=g(x)$ for $|x|<1$. Which statements are true?

options.B: A necessary condition for a solution to exist is that $g$ is an even function.
options.C: The solution, if it exists, is $u(x,y)=2\int_x^{\sqrt y}z g(z)\,dz$.
options.D: The solution, if it exists, is $u(x,y)=2\int_{\sqrt y}^{x^2}z g(z)\,dz$.

hints: The PDE implies $u(x,y)=F(x)+H(y)$. Consequently $g(x)=H^{\prime}(x^2)$.

questions.solution: The equation gives $u=F(x)+H(y)$, so the derivative data read $g(x)=H^{\prime}(x^2)$; thus $g(-x)=g(x)$ and B is necessary. Oddness is not necessary: $g\equiv1$ gives $u=y-x^2$. The value data give $F(x)=-H(x^2)$ and therefore $u=H(y)-H(x^2)=\int_{x^2}^{y}g(\sqrt s)\,ds$. For $x\ge0$, put $s=z^2$ to obtain C. For negative $x$, evenness of $g$ makes $zg(z)$ odd, so the integral from $x$ to $-x$ vanishes and the same formula remains valid. Its derivatives are $u_x=-2xg(x)$ and $u_y=g(\sqrt y)$; hence $u_{xy}=0$ and both data hold. D fails even the value datum: for $g\equiv1$, at $y=x^2$ it yields $x^4-x^2$, generally nonzero. Appropriate smoothness and boundary limits at $(0,0)$ are understood for classical data.
questions.theory: The equation $u_{xy}=0$ on a rectangle says $u_x$ is independent of $y$, or equivalently $u_y$ is independent of $x$. Integrating gives the general form $F(x)+H(y)$, with an irrelevant shared additive constant. Prescribing data on a curve can impose compatibility conditions when different curve points have the same second coordinate. On the parabola $y=x^2$, the derivative data at $x$ and $-x$ must agree, so evenness is required. This is a necessity statement, not an assertion that arbitrary nonsmooth even data produce a classical solution. The point $(0,0)$ lies on the boundary of the open PDE region; data there require the usual boundary interpretation. Change of variables must account for the two branches of the square root. Evenness of $g$ makes the integrand $zg(z)$ odd and allows one formula across both branches.

similar_questions.prompt: Solve $u_{xy}=0$ with $u(x,x^2)=0$ and $u_y(x,x^2)=x^2$.
similar_questions.solution: The data are even. Since $H^{\prime}(x^2)=x^2$, take $H^{\prime}(y)=y$ and $H(y)=y^2/2$. Then $F(x)=-x^4/2$, giving $u(x,y)=(y^2-x^4)/2$. Direct differentiation gives $u_{xy}=0$ and $u_y(x,x^2)=x^2$.

similar_questions.prompt: Can the same Cauchy problem have derivative data $g(x)=x$?

questions.prompt: Fix $\alpha\in(0,1)$. Consider $x_{k+1}=\tfrac12(x_k^2+\alpha)$ for $k=0,1,\ldots$. Its two distinct fixed points $\zeta_1,\zeta_2$ satisfy $0<\zeta_1<1<\zeta_2$. Which statements are true?

options.A: The iteration is equivalent to $x_{k+1}-\zeta_1=\tfrac12(x_k+\zeta_1)(x_k-\zeta_1)$.
options.B: The iteration is equivalent to $x_{k+1}-\zeta_1=\tfrac12(x_k+\zeta_2)(x_k-\zeta_1)$.
options.C: If $0\le x_0<\zeta_2$, then $\lim_{k\to\infty}x_k=\zeta_1$.

hints: Solve $x^2-2x+\alpha=0$ and subtract the fixed-point equation.
Check how the map acts on $[0,\zeta_1]$, $(\zeta_1,\zeta_2)$, and the interval of negative starting points.
questions.solution: The fixed points are $\zeta_1=1-\sqrt{1-\alpha}$ and $\zeta_2=1+\sqrt{1-\alpha}$. Since $2\zeta_1=\zeta_1^2+\alpha$, subtraction gives A exactly; replacing $\zeta_1$ in the first factor by $\zeta_2$ is incorrect, so B fails. Let $F(x)=(x^2+\alpha)/2$. It is increasing for $x\ge0$, and $F(x)-x=\tfrac12(x-\zeta_1)(x-\zeta_2)$. For $0\le x<\zeta_1$, $x<F(x)<\zeta_1$; for $\zeta_1<x<\zeta_2$, $\zeta_1<F(x)<x$. Thus either the iterates increase or decrease monotonically toward the only fixed point available as their limit, $\zeta_1$, proving C. If $-\zeta_2<x_0\le0$, then $0<x_1<\tfrac12(\zeta_2^2+\alpha)=\zeta_2$; C applies thereafter, proving D.
questions.theory: Fixed-point iteration $x_{k+1}=F(x_k)$ converges locally toward a fixed point $\zeta$ when $|F^{\prime}(\zeta)|<1$, while a derivative magnitude above one indicates local repulsion. Here $F^{\prime}(x)=x$, so the smaller positive fixed point attracts and the larger repels. Local derivative tests alone do not prove convergence for every starting point in a large interval. For a global result, establish an invariant interval and monotonicity of the sequence, then use the monotone convergence theorem and continuity to identify the limit as a fixed point. Factoring $F(x)-x$ reveals whether a step moves upward or downward; factoring $F(x)-\zeta$ determines whether the step crosses the target. Squaring can send negative starting values into a positive invariant interval after a single step. Boundary fixed points must be excluded where the sequence stays at the wrong limit.

similar_questions.prompt: For $x_{k+1}=(x_k^2+3/4)/2$, identify the limit when $x_0=0$.
similar_questions.solution: The fixed points are $1/2$ and $3/2$. On $[0,1/2)$, the map is larger than $x$ but smaller than $1/2$, so the iterates increase and remain bounded. Their limit must be a fixed point in $[0,1/2]$, hence is $1/2$.

similar_questions.prompt: For the same iteration, what happens if $x_0=2$?
similar_questions.solution: For $x>3/2$, $F(x)-x=\tfrac12(x-1/2)(x-3/2)>0$. Thus iterates increase and remain above two. If they had a finite limit it would be a fixed point, but both fixed points are below two. Hence the iterates diverge to $+\infty$.

With no endpoint values stated, the displayed family concerns the interior Euler–Lagrange equation; specified endpoints would determine constants. For $k=n^2$ with a positive integer $n$, all $y=a\sin(nx)$ are extremals, giving infinitely many and refuting A and D. For positive $k$ with $\sqrt k$ not an integer, the boundary conditions force $y=0$, so B holds. For $k\le0$, the affine or hyperbolic solutions likewise reduce to zero. Importantly, at $k=0$, $\sqrt k=0$ is an integer but the sole extremal is $y=0$. Thus C, as printed without excluding zero, is false. The literal correct option is B; under an additional hypothesis $k>0$, B and C would be true. questions.theory: The first variation of a quadratic functional produces a linear Euler–Lagrange boundary value problem, so its stationary functions can be classified by the spectrum of the associated differential operator. Here the Dirichlet operator $-d^2/dx^2$ on $(0,\pi)$ has positive eigenvalues $n^2$ for $n\ge1$. At an eigenvalue the homogeneous boundary value problem has a one-dimensional eigenspace, hence infinitely many scalar multiples of a nonzero extremal. Away from the spectrum its only stationary function is zero. A statement about extremals does not assert minimizers: for sufficiently large $k$ the functional can be unbounded below. Zero must not be confused with a positive integer spectral index. When a source uses $\sqrt k$ while also mentioning real $k$, state the positive, zero, and negative cases explicitly, rather than relying on an unstated parameter restriction.

questions.solution: For A, $z_x=a,z_y=b$ and the right side is $xa+yb+ab=z$. This two-parameter Clairaut family is a complete integral. For B, substitution would require $\sqrt{a^2+b^2}=ab$, which does not hold for arbitrary constants, so B fails. For C put $s=x/4-y$. Then $z=s^2$, $z_x=s/2$, $z_y=-2s$, and $xz_x+yz_y=2s^2$, while $z_xz_y=-s^2$. Their sum is $s^2=z$, and at $x=0$, $z=y^2$; C holds. For D put $s=x/4+y$. Then $xz_x+yz_y=2s^2$ and $z_xz_y=s^2$, making the right side $3s^2$, generally unequal to $z$. Hence D is false.
questions.theory: A first-order Clairaut-type PDE has the form $z=xp+yq+F(p,q)$ with $p=z_x$ and $q=z_y$. Choosing constant slopes $p=a,q=b$ gives the complete integral $z=ax+by+F(a,b)$, a two-parameter family in two independent variables. A complete integral is different from the general solution with arbitrary functions or a singular envelope obtained by eliminating parameters through derivative conditions. Prescribed data on a curve must be checked alongside the PDE: matching the curve alone does not prove a candidate solves the equation. Direct substitution is often the most reliable method for polynomial candidates and catches sign errors immediately. For the present initial curve $x=0,z=y^2$, differentiating along the curve gives $q=2y$, and the equation there forces $p=-y/2$ away from zero, selecting the minus-sign quadratic.

similar_questions.prompt: Find a complete integral of $z=xz_x+yz_y+(z_x)^2+(z_y)^2$.
similar_questions.solution: Set $z_x=a,z_y=b$. The plane family is $z=ax+by+a^2+b^2$. Its derivatives are the chosen constants, and substitution verifies the PDE for every $a,b$.

similar_questions.prompt: Find a quadratic solution of $z=xz_x+yz_y+z_xz_y$ taking $z(0,y)=4y^2$.
similar_questions.solution: Try $z=c(ax-y)^2$ with $c=4$. For $s=ax-y$, the Euler part is $2cs^2$ and the product is $-4c^2as^2$. Equality requires $c=2c-4c^2a$, so $a=1/(4c)=1/16$. Thus $z=4(x/16-y)^2$, and direct substitution verifies it.

questions.prompt: Consider a dynamical system with Lagrangian $L(q,\dot q)=T-U$, where $T=a(q)\dot q^2\ge0$, $U=U(q)$, and $a(q)>0$. Which statements are true?

options.A: The associated Lagrange equation is $\frac d{dt}\frac{\partial L}{\partial\dot q}=\frac{\partial L}{\partial q}$.
options.B: The associated Lagrange equation is $\frac d{dt}\frac{\partial L}{\partial q}=\frac{\partial L}{\partial\dot q}$.
options.C: $(q_0,\dot q_0)$ is an equilibrium position if and only if $\dot q_0=0$ and $U_q(q_0)=0$.
options.D: $(q_0,\dot q_0)$ is an equilibrium position if and only if $\dot q_0=0$ and $U_q(q_0)>0$.

hints: Recall which Lagrangian derivative is differentiated in time.
Expand the equation into $2a(q)\ddot q+a_q(q)\dot q^2+U_q(q)=0$, then impose a constant phase-space state.
questions.solution: The Euler–Lagrange equation is exactly A, so B reverses the two derivatives incorrectly. Here $\partial L/\partial\dot q=2a(q)\dot q$ and $\partial L/\partial q=a_q(q)\dot q^2-U_q(q)$. Therefore $2a(q)\ddot q+a_q(q)\dot q^2+U_q(q)=0$. In phase space put $v=\dot q$, obtaining $\dot q=v$ and $\dot v=-[a_q(q)v^2+U_q(q)]/[2a(q)]$. A constant phase-space point requires $v=0$ and then, since $a>0$, $U_q(q)=0$. These conditions are also sufficient, proving C. A strictly positive potential derivative creates a nonzero acceleration, so D fails. Equilibrium need not be stable; a maximum of $U$ can also be stationary.
questions.theory: The Lagrangian formulation derives motion from a stationary action and gives $\frac d{dt}L_{\dot q}-L_q=0$ for each generalized coordinate. The derivative with respect to velocity is the generalized momentum. When kinetic energy has a coordinate-dependent coefficient, differentiating the momentum produces both an acceleration term and a term involving the derivative of that coefficient; forgetting the latter changes the dynamics. Positivity of $a(q)$ makes the velocity Hessian nonzero, allowing the second-order equation to be solved for acceleration. An equilibrium of the corresponding autonomous first-order system means both position and velocity are constant, so its velocity is zero and the potential gradient vanishes. This is distinct from stability: curvature of the potential influences whether nearby trajectories stay close. A stationary potential maximum is an equilibrium even though it is generally unstable.

similar_questions.prompt: For $L=\tfrac12\dot q^2-\tfrac12q^2$, find the equation and equilibrium.
similar_questions.solution: Here $L_{\dot q}=\dot q$ and $L_q=-q$, so $\ddot q+q=0$. In phase space equilibrium requires $\dot q=0$ and $q=0$. The origin is the equilibrium and nearby motion is oscillatory.

similar_questions.prompt: For $L=(1+q^2)\dot q^2-q^4$, find all equilibrium points.
similar_questions.solution: The equation is $2(1+q^2)\ddot q+2q\dot q^2+4q^3=0$. At equilibrium $\dot q=0$ and $4q^3=0$, hence $(q,\dot q)=(0,0)$ is the only equilibrium.

questions.prompt: Let $X,Y$ be independent random variables with $E(X)=E(Y)=0$ and $\operatorname{Var}(X)=\operatorname{Var}(Y)=1$. Let $Z=X+Y$. Which statements are correct? The probability symbols in B and C are retained exactly as printed.

options.A: $P(|Z|>\varepsilon)\le2/\varepsilon^2$.
options.B: $P(|Z|)\le\sqrt2$.

hints: Compute $E(Z)$ and $E(Z^2)$ from independence.
Chebyshev applies to A. But $P$ requires an event as its argument, whereas the source supplies random variables in B and C.
questions.solution: Independence gives $E(Z)=0$ and $E(Z^2)=\operatorname{Var}(Z)=2$. Thus A is mathematically valid for $\varepsilon>0$ by Chebyshev. B and C, however, print $P(|Z|)$ and $P(Z)$, neither of which specifies an event; these are undefined probability expressions. The source is therefore flagged rather than replacing probability notation by expectations or variances. D is not implied by zero mean. For a counterexample let $X,Y$ independently equal $2$ with probability $1/5$ and $-1/2$ with probability $4/5$. Each has mean zero and variance one. Their sum is $4,3/2,-1$ with probabilities $1/25,8/25,16/25$, so $P(Z\le0)=16/25$ and $P(Z\ge0)=9/25$. Conditional intended reading: if B were $E|Z|\le\sqrt2$, it would hold by Cauchy–Schwarz. If C meant $E(Z)=2$, it would be false; if it meant $\operatorname{Var}(Z)=2$, it would be true. The printed source does not select those replacements.
questions.theory: For square-integrable variables, $\operatorname{Var}(X+Y)=\operatorname{Var}(X)+\operatorname{Var}(Y)+2\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)$. Independence implies zero covariance, giving variance two here, and the zero means give second moment two. Chebyshev’s inequality bounds $P(|Z-EZ|>\varepsilon)$ by $\operatorname{Var}(Z)/\varepsilon^2$ for positive $\varepsilon$. Cauchy–Schwarz separately bounds $E|Z|$ by $\sqrt{E(Z^2)}$; an expectation is a different operation from a probability. Probability notation must contain an event, such as an inequality involving the variable, while $P(Z)$ alone has no general meaning. Zero mean does not imply symmetry of a distribution or balanced mass on the positive and negative half-lines. A skew two-point distribution can satisfy both the mean and variance constraints, and independent copies provide explicit counterexamples to symmetry claims.

similar_questions.prompt: If independent $X,Y$ have zero means and variances $4,5$, bound $P(|X+Y|>6)$ and $E|X+Y|$.
similar_questions.solution: The sum has mean zero and variance nine. Chebyshev gives probability at most $9/36=1/4$. Cauchy–Schwarz gives $E|X+Y|\le\sqrt9=3$.

similar_questions.prompt: Construct a mean-zero, variance-one variable with unequal probabilities of positive and negative values.
similar_questions.solution: Take $V=2$ with probability $1/5$ and $V=-1/2$ with probability $4/5$. Its mean is $2/5-2/5=0$, and its second moment is $4/5+(1/4)(4/5)=1$. Yet $P(V>0)=1/5$ differs from $P(V<0)=4/5$.

questions.prompt: Let $n>1$ and let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ satisfy $E(X_i)=0$, $E(X_i^2)=1$ for every $i$, and $E(X_iX_j)=\rho$ for all $i\ne j$. Which statements are true?

options.A: $\rho=0$ if and only if $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ are independent.
options.B: $\operatorname{Var}(X_1+\cdots+X_n)=n$ if and only if $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ are independent.
options.C: $\operatorname{Var}(X_1+\cdots+X_n)=n$ if and only if $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ are pairwise

hints: Expand the variance using the common off-diagonal covariance.
Zero covariance is weaker than independence. The source leaves the property after “pairwise” in C unstated.
questions.solution: The variance is $n+2\binom n2\rho=n+n(n-1)\rho$. Since $n>1$, it equals $n$ exactly when $\rho=0$, so D is unambiguously true. Independence implies these equalities but their converses fail. For $n=2$, take $X_1=G$ and $X_2=(G^2-1)/\sqrt2$, where $G\sim N(0,1)$. They have zero means and unit variances because $E(G^2)=1,E(G^4)=3$, and covariance $(E(G^3)-E(G))/\sqrt2=0$. They are dependent since the second is a function of the first. This refutes A and B, and also refutes C if its missing word is “independent.” The actual option C terminates after “pairwise,” with no property supplied. If completed as “uncorrelated,” C would instead be true. Because these plausible completions change the answer set, the source is marked ambiguous with no assigned correct_options. Conditional intended answer for “pairwise independent” would be D alone.
questions.theory: Covariance describes a second-moment relationship and is not a general test of independence. Pairwise independence implies pairwise zero covariance when second moments exist, but uncorrelated variables can be dependent. Joint independence is stronger than pairwise independence. For a jointly Gaussian vector, zero cross-covariances do imply independence, but that extra hypothesis is absent here. The variance of a sum is the sum of variances plus twice every distinct-pair covariance. Under a common covariance $\rho$, all cross terms combine into $n(n-1)\rho$. The positive-semidefinite covariance matrix also imposes $-1/(n-1)\le\rho\le1$, although that bound is not needed for D. A quadratic function of a symmetric variable provides a practical uncorrelated-dependent example. An incomplete multiple-choice option cannot be silently completed, particularly when different completions have different truth values.

similar_questions.prompt: If four unit-variance, zero-mean variables have common covariance $1/3$, compute the variance of their sum.
similar_questions.solution: The formula gives $4+4(3)(1/3)=8$. The cross terms account for the additional four units of variance.

similar_questions.prompt: For $G\sim N(0,1)$, show that $G$ and $(G^2-1)/\sqrt2$ are uncorrelated but dependent.
similar_questions.solution: The second variable has mean zero and variance $(3-2+1)/2=1$. Covariance with $G$ is $(E G^3-E G)/\sqrt2=0$. It is nevertheless a deterministic nonconstant function of $G$, so they are dependent; for example, its value determines $G^2$.

questions.prompt: Consider a Markov chain with a countable state space $S$. Identify the correct statements.

options.A: If the chain is aperiodic and irreducible, then there exists a stationary distribution.
options.B: If the chain is aperiodic and irreducible, then there is at most one stationary distribution.
options.C: If $S$ is finite, then there exists a stationary distribution.
options.D: If $S$ is finite, then there is exactly one stationary distribution.

hints: For infinite irreducible chains, existence requires positive recurrence, not just aperiodicity.
Finite chains always have stationary distributions, but two absorbing states already destroy uniqueness.
questions.solution: A is false: the lazy symmetric random walk on $\mathbb Z$, with transitions to $i$ of probability $1/2$ and to $i\pm1$ of probability $1/4$, is irreducible and aperiodic but null recurrent and has no stationary probability distribution. Directly, stationarity requires $2\pi_i=\pi_{i-1}+\pi_{i+1}$, so successive differences are constant; no nonnegative summable solution on all integers can have total mass one. B is true: an irreducible countable chain has at most one stationary probability distribution, and one exists exactly when it is positive recurrent. C holds because a finite stochastic matrix has a stationary probability vector, equivalently at least one finite closed recurrent class. D fails for the identity transition matrix on two states: every probability vector is stationary.
questions.theory: A stationary distribution is a nonnegative probability row vector $\pi$ satisfying $\pi P=\pi$. For an irreducible countable-state chain, a stationary probability distribution exists precisely under positive recurrence and is then unique. Null recurrence or transience can prevent existence even when the chain is irreducible and aperiodic. Aperiodicity concerns possible return times and is relevant to convergence toward equilibrium, not to existence of a stationary distribution. Finite chains always contain closed communicating classes and always admit at least one stationary distribution. Each finite closed irreducible class supplies a stationary distribution supported on it; convex combinations across distinct closed classes generally give many distributions. Finite irreducibility guarantees uniqueness, but finiteness alone does not. A self-loop at one state of an irreducible class forces that class to be aperiodic.

similar_questions.prompt: Find all stationary distributions for $P=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$.
similar_questions.solution: Every vector $(a,1-a)$ with $0\le a\le1$ satisfies $\pi P=\pi$. The states are distinct absorbing closed classes, so there are infinitely many stationary distributions.

similar_questions.prompt: Find the stationary distribution for $P=\begin{pmatrix}1/2&1/2\\1/4&3/4\end{pmatrix}$.
similar_questions.solution: Writing $\pi=(a,1-a)$, stationarity gives $a=a/2+(1-a)/4$, hence $3a=1$ and $a=1/3$. Thus $\pi=(1/3,2/3)$, uniquely because the finite chain is irreducible.

questions.prompt: Consider the Markov chain with $P=\begin{pmatrix}0&0&1/2&0&1/2\\0&1/2&0&1/2&0\\1/2&0&0&0&1/2\\0&1/2&0&1/2&0\\1/2&0&1/2&0&0\end{pmatrix}$. Let $\pi=(1/5,1/5,1/5,1/5,1/5)$. Which statements are correct?

options.A: $\pi$ is a stationary distribution.
options.B: If $\eta$ is a stationary distribution, then $\eta=\pi$.
options.C: The Markov chain is periodic.

hints: Inspect the column sums, and separate the communicating classes.
The closed classes are $\{1,3,5\}$ and $\{2,4\}$. In the first, returns of lengths two and three occur; in the second there are self-loops.
questions.solution: The matrix is doubly stochastic, so multiplication of its uniform probability vector by $P$ again gives the uniform vector, proving A. There are two disjoint closed communicating classes, $\{1,3,5\}$ and $\{2,4\}$, so D is false. The stationary distributions are $(a/3,(1-a)/2,a/3,(1-a)/2,a/3)$ for $0\le a\le1$; the stated $\pi$ corresponds to $a=3/5$ and is not unique, so B is false. Within the three-state class one can return in two steps (e.g. $1\to3\to1$) and in three ($1\to3\to5\to1$), giving period $\gcd(2,3)=1$. States two and four have self-loops, also period one. All states are aperiodic, so C is false.
questions.theory: Communication means mutual reachability through positive-probability paths. A chain is irreducible when all states communicate; a closed class has no outgoing transition to another class. Stationarity and irreducibility are distinct: a reducible chain can have a stationary distribution, and even a uniform one if its matrix is doubly stochastic. Each finite closed irreducible class has its own normalized stationary vector, and mixtures of these vectors form global stationary distributions. The period of a state is the greatest common divisor of all positive return lengths, not simply its shortest return time. A class with two-step returns can still be aperiodic if it also has three-step returns. States in the same communicating class share the period, but distinct closed classes must be checked separately. Self-loops immediately give period one.

similar_questions.prompt: For a random walk that moves uniformly to either of the other vertices of a triangle, determine the period and stationary distribution.
similar_questions.solution: The transition matrix has zero diagonal and off-diagonal entries $1/2$. A vertex has return paths of lengths two and three, so its period is one. Column sums are one, and the unique stationary distribution is uniform $(1/3,1/3,1/3)$.

similar_questions.prompt: Find stationary distributions for a chain consisting of two disjoint two-state alternating cycles.
similar_questions.solution: Each cycle has uniform stationary distribution on its two vertices and period two. Assign total mass $a$ to the first cycle and $1-a$ to the second, giving $(a/2,a/2,(1-a)/2,(1-a)/2)$ for $0\le a\le1$. The chain is reducible and stationary distributions are not unique.

questions.prompt: Suppose $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ are i.i.d. with characteristic function $\phi(t;\theta)=E[e^{itX_1}]$, where $\theta\in\mathbb R^k$ is the distribution parameter. Let $Z=X_1+\cdots+X_n$. For which distributions of $X_1$ is the characteristic function of $Z$ again of the form $\phi(t;\alpha)$ for a parameter $\alpha\in\mathbb R^k$?

options.A: Negative Binomial
options.B: Geometric
options.C: Hypergeometric

hints: The characteristic function of the sum is $\phi(t;\theta)^n$. Seek a family closed under sums of independent members with the same parameter.
Negative binomial counts add their size parameters while retaining the success probability. Summing geometric variables usually changes the family.
questions.solution: Use the negative-binomial convention counting failures before $r$ successes: $\phi(t;r,p)=[p/(1-(1-p)e^{it})]^r$. Raising to the $n$th power gives the same formula with $r$ replaced by $nr$, so A is true. A geometric variable is the case $r=1$; for nondegenerate $p$ and $n\ge2$ the sum has size $n$ and is not geometric, so B fails. Hypergeometric laws describe draws without replacement from a fixed finite population; independent sums do not in general remain hypergeometric. For instance, two independent Bernoulli$(1/2)$ variables are individually hypergeometric with population two, one success and one draw, but their sum has probabilities $(1/4,1/2,1/4)$, which no finite-population hypergeometric with this support and mean reproduces. Indeed, for a hypergeometric with population size $N$, successes $K$, and draws $m$, this support forces $\min(K,m)=2$ and mean one forces $N=mK$. If $m=2$, its variance is $(K-1)/(2K-1)<1/2$; if $K=2$, symmetry gives $(m-1)/(2m-1)<1/2$. Both contradict the variance $1/2$ of this sum. Two independent uniform variables on $\{0,1\}$ give the same triangular probabilities rather than a uniform law, refuting D. The question concerns family closure for general sample sizes; $n=1$ alone is tautological.
questions.theory: Characteristic functions uniquely determine distributions and turn independent sums into products. Thus convolution closure can be tested by whether a product remains within a specified parametric family. The negative-binomial family is closed under independent sums with common success probability: size parameters add, under either the failure-count or total-trial convention. A geometric distribution is only the size-one subfamily, so a sum generally leaves it. Finite-support families require attention to the whole probability shape, not just support or mean. Discrete uniform sums commonly produce triangular or trapezoidal mass functions. Hypergeometric sampling has a finite-population variance correction absent from independent Bernoulli sums. Closure is a family-level assertion for general nondegenerate parameters and sample sizes; exceptional degenerate parameters or the identity case $n=1$ do not establish the general property.

similar_questions.prompt: If independent $X,Y$ are negative binomial failure counts with sizes $2,5$ and common success probability $p$, find $X+Y$.
similar_questions.solution: Their characteristic functions are powers two and five of the same factor $p/[1-(1-p)e^{it}]$. Multiplication gives power seven, so the sum is negative binomial with size seven and success probability $p$.

similar_questions.prompt: Find the distribution of the sum of two independent uniform variables on $\{0,1\}$.
similar_questions.solution: The four equally probable pairs are $(0,0),(0,1),(1,0),(1,1)$. They give masses $1/4,1/2,1/4$ at $0,1,2$. The middle value is twice as likely as either endpoint, so the sum is not discrete uniform.

questions.prompt: Let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be i.i.d. with density $f(x\mid\theta)=\theta/x^{\theta+1}$ for $x>1$, where $\theta>1$ is unknown. Which estimators of $\theta$ are consistent?

options.A: $\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nX_i$.
options.B: $\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\log X_i$.
options.C: $\frac n{\sum_{i=1}^nX_i}$.

hints: Compute $E(X)$ and the distribution of $\log X$.
$\log X$ is exponential with rate $\theta$, so its sample mean tends to $1/\theta$. Apply the continuous mapping theorem.
questions.solution: For $\theta>1$, $E(X)=\theta\int_1^\infty x^{-\theta}\,dx=\theta/(\theta-1)$. Also $Y=\log X$ has density $\theta e^{-\theta y}$ for $y>0$, so $E(Y)=1/\theta$. The strong law gives $\overline X\to\theta/(\theta-1)$ and $\overline{\log X}\to1/\theta$. Their reciprocals tend respectively to $(\theta-1)/\theta$ and $\theta$. Thus only D is consistent throughout the parameter space. A happens to converge to $\theta$ at the isolated value $\theta=2$, but an estimator is called consistent for the family only when it works for every allowed parameter; that coincidence does not make A a consistent estimator of the general parameter. A finite first moment suffices for this law of large numbers, so finite variance is not required.
questions.theory: Consistency means that for each fixed allowed parameter, the estimator converges in probability to that parameter as sample size increases. A sample average converges to the population expectation when the first absolute moment is finite, not automatically to whichever parameter labels the density. Method-of-moments estimators invert the relationship between the expectation and parameter. Transformations can simplify the model: logarithms of Pareto variables are exponential, making the rate accessible through the reciprocal sample mean. The continuous mapping theorem permits taking reciprocals because the limiting mean is positive and nonzero. Strong almost-sure convergence implies convergence in probability. Heavy tails may yield infinite variance for some parameters while still allowing the strong law because the first moment exists. An estimator that succeeds only at one exceptional parameter is not consistent across the entire stated family.

similar_questions.prompt: For Pareto density $\theta x^{-\theta-1}$, derive a consistent estimator from $\overline X$ when $\theta>1$.
similar_questions.solution: The expectation is $m=\theta/(\theta-1)$. Solve for $\theta=m/(m-1)$. Since $\overline X\to m>1$, continuous mapping gives $\widehat\theta=\overline X/(\overline X-1)\to\theta$.

similar_questions.prompt: For i.i.d. exponential variables with rate $\lambda>0$, show that $n/\sum X_i$ is consistent.
similar_questions.solution: The sample mean converges almost surely to $1/\lambda$ by the strong law. Its positive reciprocal therefore converges almost surely to $\lambda$, proving consistency.

questions.prompt: Let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be i.i.d. with $p(x\mid\theta)=\theta^x(1-\theta)^{1-x}$, $x=0,1$, and $0\le\theta\le1/2$. Then

options.A: The method-of-moments estimator of $\theta$ is $\frac1{2n}\sum_{i=1}^nX_i$.
options.B: The MLE of $\theta$ is $\min_{1\le i\le n}X_i$.
options.C: The method-of-moments estimator of $\theta$ is $\min_{1\le i\le n}X_i$.

hints: The Bernoulli expectation is $\theta$, with no factor two.
First maximize the binomial likelihood without the restriction; then enforce the upper boundary $1/2$.
questions.solution: Write $s=\sum_iX_i$. The likelihood is $L(\theta)=\theta^s(1-\theta)^{n-s}$. For $0<s<n$, the derivative of its logarithm is $s/\theta-(n-s)/(1-\theta)$, zero at $\theta=s/n$. The log likelihood is concave, so the constrained maximizer is $s/n$ if $s/n\le1/2$, and $1/2$ otherwise. The all-zero sample maximizes at zero, and the all-one sample at $1/2$, giving the same formula. Thus D holds and B fails. The moment equation is $\overline X=E(X)=\theta$, so its ordinary moment solution is $\overline X$, neither the half-mean in A nor the sample minimum in C. When $\overline X>1/2$, the raw moment equation has no solution inside the restricted parameter interval; projecting a moment estimate is an additional convention, not either printed claim.
questions.theory: Maximum likelihood selects a parameter in the actual allowed parameter space that maximizes the observed-data probability. For a Bernoulli sample, the sum of observations is sufficient and the unconstrained maximizer is the sample proportion. A closed parameter constraint can push that maximizer to a boundary; concavity of the log likelihood makes the clipping rule easy to justify. Boundary samples should be treated directly because logarithmic derivatives contain division by zero at the endpoints. The method of moments instead equates sample and population moments. It does not automatically coincide with maximum likelihood under constraints, and a moment equation can have no parameter-space solution for some samples. The sample minimum discards most information about the number of successes and generally cannot maximize this likelihood. Always distinguish the unconstrained estimate, the constrained maximizer, and any separately defined projected moment estimate.

similar_questions.prompt: A Bernoulli parameter is restricted to $[0,0.3]$. What is the MLE from seven successes in ten trials?
similar_questions.solution: The unconstrained estimate is $0.7$. The likelihood increases up to $0.7$, so throughout the allowed interval its maximum is at the upper endpoint. The constrained MLE is $0.3$.

similar_questions.prompt: For a Bernoulli parameter restricted to $[0.2,0.8]$, find the MLE from one success in ten trials.
similar_questions.solution: The unconstrained estimate $0.1$ lies below the parameter interval. Concavity implies the likelihood decreases throughout $[0.2,0.8]$, so the MLE is its lower endpoint $0.2$.

questions.prompt: Let $X$ have density $f(x\mid\theta)=2x/\theta^2$ for $0<x<\theta$, where $\theta>0$ is unknown. Which are $100(1-\alpha)\%$ confidence intervals for $\theta$?

options.A: $[X,X/\sqrt\alpha]$.
options.C: $[\frac{\sqrt2}{\sqrt{2-\alpha}}X,\frac{\sqrt2}{\sqrt\alpha}X]$.

hints: The pivot $T=X/\theta$ has distribution function $P(T\le t)=t^2$ on $[0,1]$.
Translate each coverage event into bounds on $T$. For C, the squared bounds are $\alpha/2$ and $1-\alpha/2$.
questions.solution: For $0<\alpha<1$, the pivot $T=X/\theta$ has CDF $t^2$ on $[0,1]$. A covers exactly when $\sqrt\alpha\le T\le1$, with probability $1-\alpha$, so A is valid. C covers when $\sqrt{\alpha/2}\le T\le\sqrt{1-\alpha/2}$, whose probability is $(1-\alpha/2)-\alpha/2=1-\alpha$, so C is valid. B covers when $1/2\le T\le1$ and has constant coverage $3/4$, matching the requested level only in the special case $\alpha=1/4$, not for general $\alpha$. D has coverage zero because $X<\theta$ almost surely. The selected general intervals are A and C.
questions.theory: A confidence interval is a random interval whose coverage probability equals the prescribed confidence level for every value of the unknown parameter. It is a repeated-sampling probability statement about the interval, not a posterior probability assigned to a fixed parameter. A pivot has a distribution independent of the unknown parameter, enabling exact interval construction. In a scale family, the ratio $X/\theta$ often provides such a pivot. Quantile inequalities must be rearranged carefully because the parameter occurs in the denominator and all terms are positive. One-sided and equal-tail constructions can both have the same exact coverage, so a question may have multiple valid intervals. An interval independent of $\alpha$ generally has a fixed confidence level and cannot represent every requested level. Open versus closed endpoints does not affect coverage for a continuous distribution.

similar_questions.prompt: If $X\sim\operatorname{Uniform}(0,\theta)$, find an exact $1-\alpha$ interval of the form $[X,cX]$.
similar_questions.solution: The pivot $X/\theta$ is uniform on $(0,1)$. Coverage of $[X,cX]$ is $P(X/\theta\ge1/c)=1-1/c$. Set $1/c=\alpha$, giving $[X,X/\alpha]$.

similar_questions.prompt: For density $3x^2/\theta^3$ on $(0,\theta)$, find an exact equal-tail $1-\alpha$ interval.
similar_questions.solution: The pivot CDF is $t^3$. Its equal-tail bounds are $(\alpha/2)^{1/3}$ and $(1-\alpha/2)^{1/3}$. Rearranging gives $[X/(1-\alpha/2)^{1/3},X/(\alpha/2)^{1/3}]$, with coverage exactly $1-\alpha$.

questions.prompt: $X$ has a binomial distribution with parameters $n,p$, where $n$ is given and $p$ has the uniform prior on $[0,1]$. Consider squared-error loss and observation $X=n$. Identify the correct statements.

options.A: The Bayes estimate of $p$ is $(n+1)/(n+2)$.
options.B: The Bayes estimate of $p$ is $2^{-1/(n+1)}$.
options.C: The median of the posterior distribution of $p$ is $2^{-1/(n+1)}$.
options.D: The median of the posterior distribution of $p$ is $(n+1)/(n+2)$.

hints: The likelihood at $X=n$ is proportional to $p^n$. Normalize it on $[0,1]$.
Squared-error loss selects the posterior mean; a posterior median solves the posterior CDF equation $F(m)=1/2$.
questions.solution: The uniform prior and all-success likelihood give posterior density $\pi(p\mid X=n)=(n+1)p^n$, $0<p<1$, a Beta$(n+1,1)$ law. Its mean is $(n+1)\int_0^1p^{n+1}dp=(n+1)/(n+2)$, which is the Bayes estimate under squared-error loss, proving A. Its CDF is $F(p)=p^{n+1}$, so its median satisfies $m^{n+1}=1/2$, yielding $m=2^{-1/(n+1)}$ and proving C. For the standard binomial trial count $n\ge1$, mean and median differ, so B and D are false. The distinction comes from the loss function, not from choosing whichever posterior center is easier to calculate.
questions.theory: Bayesian updating multiplies the prior density by the likelihood and normalizes the result. The Beta$(a,b)$ family is conjugate to a binomial likelihood: observing $x$ successes in $n$ trials produces Beta$(a+x,b+n-x)$. The posterior mean is $(a+x)/(a+b+n)$, but the posterior median generally has a different value. Under squared-error loss the posterior expected loss decomposes into posterior variance plus the square of the distance from the posterior mean, making that mean the unique optimal action. Under absolute-error loss a posterior median is optimal instead. Beta$(a,1)$ has a particularly simple CDF $p^a$, enabling an explicit median. Do not confuse a Bayes estimator with the maximum-likelihood estimator, which is one after observing all successes and does not include prior smoothing.

similar_questions.prompt: With a uniform prior and $X=0$ in $n$ Bernoulli trials, find the squared-loss Bayes estimate.
similar_questions.solution: The posterior is Beta$(1,n+1)$, with density $(n+1)(1-p)^n$. Its mean is $1/(n+2)$, hence the squared-loss Bayes estimate is $1/(n+2)$.

similar_questions.prompt: With prior Beta$(2,3)$ and eight successes in ten trials, find the posterior and squared-loss estimate.
similar_questions.solution: Conjugacy gives Beta$(2+8,3+2)=$Beta$(10,5)$. Its posterior mean, and squared-loss Bayes estimate, is $10/(10+5)=2/3$.

questions.prompt: Let $X_1,X_2,X_3$ be a random sample from Uniform$(0,\theta)$. The prior on $\theta$ is Uniform$(0,1)$, and $X_{(3)}=\max\{X_1,X_2,X_3\}$. Consider squared-error loss. Which statements are necessarily true?

options.A: The Bayes estimator of $\theta$ is unique.
options.B: $1/X_{(3)}$ is a Bayes estimator of $\theta$.
options.C: $X_{(3)}$ is a Bayes estimator of $\theta$.

hints: For observed maximum $m$, the likelihood is $\theta^{-3}\mathbf1_{\{m<\theta<1\}}$.
Normalize this density and compute its mean. Strict convexity of squared loss gives uniqueness.
questions.solution: Almost surely $0<m=X_{(3)}<1$. The posterior density is $c\theta^{-3}$ for $m<\theta<1$, where $c^{-1}=\int_m^1\theta^{-3}d\theta=(m^{-2}-1)/2$, so $c=2m^2/(1-m^2)$. Its mean is $c\int_m^1\theta^{-2}d\theta=c(m^{-1}-1)=2m/(1+m)$. The posterior expected squared loss equals its variance plus $(a-E[\theta\mid X])^2$, giving a unique minimizing action and proving A. None of B,C,D equals $2m/(1+m)$ for almost all observations. In particular $1/m>1$ is outside the prior support, and $2m/(1+m)>m$ for $0<m<1$. Equality at isolated observations does not make an estimator a Bayes rule.
questions.theory: When a parameter controls the support of a density, the likelihood includes a support indicator that depends on the observed extreme values. For a Uniform$(0,\theta)$ sample of size $r$, the likelihood is proportional to $\theta^{-r}$ on $\theta$ above the sample maximum. A bounded uniform prior further truncates that support at its upper endpoint. Posterior normalization must use these data-dependent integration limits. Under squared-error loss, the posterior mean is optimal and its uniqueness follows from the positive quadratic coefficient in the expected loss, provided the second moment is finite. A Bayes rule is understood up to changes on observations of prior-predictive probability zero. A statistic that occasionally matches the posterior mean is not thereby a Bayes estimator. The posterior mean lies between the observed maximum and the prior upper bound, a useful check on any proposed formula.

similar_questions.prompt: For one observation from Uniform$(0,\theta)$ with prior Uniform$(0,1)$, find the posterior mean when $X=x$.
similar_questions.solution: The posterior is proportional to $1/\theta$ for $x<\theta<1$. Its normalizing integral is $-\log x$. Its mean is $\int_x^1d\theta/(-\log x)=(1-x)/(-\log x)$.

similar_questions.prompt: For three observations with prior Uniform$(0,b)$, find the squared-loss Bayes estimate from maximum $m<b$.
similar_questions.solution: The posterior normalizing integral is $(m^{-2}-b^{-2})/2$, while its first-moment integral is $m^{-1}-b^{-1}$. Their ratio is $2mb/(m+b)$, the unique posterior mean and Bayes estimate.

questions.prompt: Consider the Gauss–Markov model $\mathbf Y_{n\times1}=\mathbf X_{n\times p}\boldsymbol\beta_{p\times1}+\boldsymbol\varepsilon_{n\times1}$ with $E(\boldsymbol\varepsilon)=0$, $\operatorname{Dispersion}(\boldsymbol\varepsilon)=\sigma^2I_n$, and $p<n$. Which statements are correct?

options.A: The least-squares estimate of $\boldsymbol\beta$ is unique.
options.B: The least-squares estimate of an estimable linear function of $\boldsymbol\beta$ is unique.
options.C: The least-squares estimate of $\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta$ is unique.

hints: The condition $p<n$ does not guarantee full column rank.
All least-squares coefficient solutions differ by a vector in $\ker\mathbf X$, while their fitted vectors are the same orthogonal projection.
questions.solution: Least squares projects $\mathbf Y$ orthogonally onto $\operatorname{col}(\mathbf X)$; therefore $\mathbf X\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}$ is always unique, proving C. If $\widehat\beta_1,\widehat\beta_2$ are minimizers, their difference lies in $\ker\mathbf X$. A linear function $c^T\beta$ is estimable exactly when $c\in\operatorname{row}(\mathbf X)=(\ker\mathbf X)^\perp$, so $c^T\widehat\beta_1=c^T\widehat\beta_2$, proving B. The inequality $p<n$ does not imply rank $p$. For example with $n=3,p=2$ and two identical columns $(1,1,1)^T$, coefficient sums are determined but individual coefficients are not: A fails. Here $\mathbf X^T\mathbf X=\begin{pmatrix}3&3\\3&3\end{pmatrix}$ has determinant zero, refuting D. Full column rank, if additionally supplied, would make A and D true.
questions.theory: The Gauss–Markov assumptions provide unbiased errors with a common uncorrelated variance but do not require normally distributed errors. Least squares is geometrically an orthogonal projection onto the design matrix’s column space. That projection is unique even for a rank-deficient design, while coefficient representations of it may be nonunique. An estimable linear function of the parameter is one whose coefficient vector belongs to the row space of the design; it cannot change when a null-space vector is added to the parameter. This algebraic characterization guarantees uniqueness of its least-squares estimate. The Gram matrix $X^TX$ is positive semidefinite and is positive definite precisely when columns of $X$ are linearly independent. Having more observations than parameters is necessary for some full-rank settings but does not establish independence of columns. Always check rank instead of relying on matrix dimensions.

similar_questions.prompt: For $X=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}$, describe least-squares coefficient estimates and fitted values.
similar_questions.solution: The model mean is $(\beta_1+\beta_2)\mathbf1$. Least squares requires $\widehat\beta_1+\widehat\beta_2=\overline Y$, leaving infinitely many coefficient pairs. The fitted vector is uniquely $\overline Y\mathbf1$.

similar_questions.prompt: In this same design, is $\beta_1-\beta_2$ estimable?
similar_questions.solution: The row space is spanned by $(1,1)$. The contrast vector $(1,-1)$ is not in that space and varies when $(t,-t)$ is added to the coefficients without changing the mean. Hence the difference is not estimable, whereas the sum is.

questions.prompt: Let $p>1$ and $0\le\rho<1$. In multiple regression with predictors $X_1,\ldots,X_p$ and response $Y$, suppose every correlation between $Y$ and $X_i$ equals $\rho$, and every correlation between distinct predictors equals $\rho$. Which statements are correct?

options.A: The multiple correlation between $Y$ and $(X_1,\ldots,X_p)$ is at least $\rho$.
options.B: The multiple correlation equals $\rho$ if $\rho=0$.
options.C: The multiple correlation equals $\rho$ only if $\rho=0$.
options.D: The multiple correlation tends to one as $p\to\infty$.

hints: The predictor correlation matrix is $(1-\rho)I_p+\rho\mathbf1\mathbf1^T$.
Its eigenvalue on $\mathbf1$ is $1+(p-1)\rho$, so $R^2=p\rho^2/[1+(p-1)\rho]$.
questions.solution: Let $R_X=(1-\rho)I_p+\rho J_p$ and $r=\rho\mathbf1$. Since $R_X\mathbf1=[1+(p-1)\rho]\mathbf1$, the squared multiple correlation is $R^2=r^TR_X^{-1}r=p\rho^2/[1+(p-1)\rho]$. The factor $p/[1+(p-1)\rho]\ge1$, so $R\ge\rho$, proving A. If $\rho=0$, $R=0$, proving B. If $0<\rho<1$, that factor is strictly greater than one because $(p-1)(1-\rho)>0$, so $R>\rho$; thus equality occurs only at zero and C holds. For fixed positive $\rho$, $R^2\to\rho$ and $R\to\sqrt\rho<1$; at $\rho=0$ the limit is zero. Hence D is false.
questions.theory: The multiple correlation is the nonnegative correlation between a response and its best linear prediction from the predictors. For standardized variables with a nonsingular predictor correlation matrix, its square is $r^TR_X^{-1}r$, where $r$ collects response–predictor correlations. Equicorrelation matrices split into the all-ones direction and its orthogonal complement, with eigenvalues $1+(p-1)\rho$ and $1-\rho$ respectively. This structure makes inverse calculations straightforward without a large matrix inversion. Adding predictors cannot worsen the optimal linear fit, but highly correlated predictors provide overlapping information, so the improvement can approach a limit below perfect prediction. Equality of a multiple and a simple correlation needs separate treatment at zero. When taking $p\to\infty$, keep $\rho$ fixed unless the source specifies another limiting scheme. Remember to take the square root after deriving $R^2$.

similar_questions.prompt: With three predictors and all specified correlations $\rho=1/2$, calculate the multiple correlation.
similar_questions.solution: The formula gives $R^2=3(1/4)/(1+2(1/2))=3/8$. Thus $R=\sqrt{3/8}$, which exceeds the individual correlation $1/2$.

similar_questions.prompt: If all correlations equal $1/4$, find the limiting multiple correlation as predictor count increases.
similar_questions.solution: Here $R^2=p/16\,/\,[1+(p-1)/4]$, which tends to $1/4$. Therefore $R\to1/2$, not one.

questions.prompt: Let $n>2$ and $0<\theta<\pi/2$. Let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be i.i.d. normal with mean zero and variance $\sigma^2>0$. For $i=1,\ldots,n$, define $Y_{2i-1}=X_i\cos\theta$, $Y_{2i}=X_i\sin\theta$. Let $Z^T=(Y_1,Y_2,\ldots,Y_{2n})$ and $V^T=(X_1,Y_1,Y_2,X_2,Y_3,Y_4,\ldots,X_n,Y_{2n-1},Y_{2n})$. Which statements are correct?

options.A: $Z^T$ has a multivariate normal distribution.
options.B: There exists a constant $C$ such that $CZ^TZ$ has a chi-square distribution.
options.C: $V^T$ has a multivariate normal distribution.

hints: Both vectors are linear transformations of the normal vector $(X_1,\ldots,X_n)^T$. A multivariate normal can have singular covariance.
Use $\cos^2\theta+\sin^2\theta=1$ to simplify the two squared norms, then use a chi-square inverse moment.
questions.solution: Both $Z$ and $V$ are fixed linear transformations of the independent normal vector $X$, so every linear combination of their coordinates is normal. Thus A and C hold, even though their covariance matrices are singular. For each $i$, $Y_{2i-1}^2+Y_{2i}^2=X_i^2$. Consequently $Z^TZ=\sum_iX_i^2$ and $C=1/\sigma^2$ makes $CZ^TZ\sim\chi_n^2$, proving B. Likewise $V^TV=2\sum_iX_i^2=2\sigma^2W$, $W\sim\chi_n^2$. The gamma integral gives $E(W^{-1})=1/(n-2)$ for $n>2$, so $E[1/(V^TV)]=1/[2\sigma^2(n-2)]<\infty$, proving D. All four statements are valid.
questions.theory: A vector is multivariate normal if every real linear combination of its coordinates is a univariate normal variable, allowing degenerate combinations with zero variance. Consequently any fixed linear transformation of a multivariate normal vector is still multivariate normal; invertibility and a nonsingular covariance are unnecessary. A singular Gaussian law may lack a density in the full ambient space but remains a valid multivariate distribution. The sum of squares of $n$ independent standard normals has a chi-square distribution with $n$ degrees of freedom. Repeated coordinates or correlated linear copies do not automatically increase those degrees of freedom; simplify the quadratic form first. The chi-square law is Gamma$(n/2,2)$, whose inverse first moment exists exactly for $n>2$ and equals $1/(n-2)$. Finiteness is determined by density behavior near zero, not its exponentially decaying tail.

similar_questions.prompt: If $X_1,X_2$ are independent standard normals, is $(X_1,2X_1,X_2)$ multivariate normal?
similar_questions.solution: Yes. Every linear combination is $(a+2b)X_1+cX_2$, which is normal. Its covariance is singular because the second coordinate is twice the first, but singularity does not remove multivariate normality.

similar_questions.prompt: For four independent $N(0,9)$ variables, find $E[1/\sum X_i^2]$.
similar_questions.solution: Write $\sum X_i^2=9W$ with $W\sim\chi_4^2$. Since $E(W^{-1})=1/(4-2)=1/2$, the expectation is $1/(9\cdot2)=1/18$.
